subtopic_detail: Nodular acne with early scarring that has not responded to four months of oral tetracycline and topical therapy
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 19 year old woman who has been using adapalene with benzoyl peroxide each night and taking doxycycline 100 mg daily for the past four months. She has taken the tablets consistently and has not missed applications.

Her face and upper back carry deep tender nodules that last several weeks, and she has developed several small depressed scars on both cheeks since her last visit. She has stopped going to her university tutorials and describes feeling flat about her appearance, though she denies any thoughts of self harm. Her periods are regular, she is not sexually active, and she takes no other medication. There is no hirsutism, no acanthosis nigricans and no galactorrhoea, and her body mass index is 22 kg/m2.

data_table.Examination: Deep inflammatory nodules over both cheeks, jawline and upper back, several atrophic scars on the cheeks, no comedonal predominance, no hirsutism
data_table.Treatment history: Adapalene with benzoyl peroxide nightly and doxycycline 100 mg daily for 4 months with good adherence

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Continue the current doxycycline and topical regimen for a further six months before any change
options.rationale: Response to an oral tetracycline is assessed at around three months and prolonged courses beyond six months add resistance risk without further benefit in nodular disease. Continuing unchanged also allows further permanent scarring to accumulate (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

options.text: Substitute minocycline for the doxycycline while keeping the topical treatment unchanged
options.rationale: Switching within the tetracycline class rarely rescues true treatment failure and minocycline carries added risks of hyperpigmentation, drug induced lupus and hypersensitivity. It is not favoured as a first or second line agent in Australian guidance (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

options.text: Add a combined oral contraceptive pill and reassess her skin again in a further three months
options.rationale: Hormonal therapy helps inflammatory acne with a hormonal pattern but takes three to six cycles to work and is a weaker choice when nodules are already scarring. It would be a reasonable addition in milder disease or where contraception is also wanted (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

options.text: Refer her to a dermatologist for assessment for a course of oral isotretinoin treatment
options.rationale: Nodular acne that is scarring, causing psychological distress, or failing conventional oral and topical therapy is the recognised indication for isotretinoin, which in Australia is prescribed by a dermatologist under an authority listing. Referral rather than further temporising limits the number of permanent scars she accrues (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

options.text: Intensify the topical regimen with the addition of a topical clindamycin preparation twice daily
options.rationale: Topical antibiotics act on superficial inflammatory lesions and cannot reach the deep nodules driving her scarring, and they should never be used without benzoyl peroxide because of resistance. This step suits mild to moderate papulopustular disease (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology).

explanation.summary: Acne severity for treatment purposes is judged by lesion type and by consequences rather than by lesion counts alone, so scarring and psychological impact move a patient up the ladder regardless of how the skin scores. Nodular disease that persists after an adequate trial of an oral tetracycline with a topical retinoid and benzoyl peroxide is the standard trigger for isotretinoin referral. Isotretinoin requires pregnancy prevention with reliable contraception and monthly pregnancy testing in people who can become pregnant, along with baseline and interval lipids and liver function. Mood should be asked about before and during treatment, though a causal link with depression has not been established. Early referral is the main lever available to prevent permanent scarring.
key_points: Assess response to an oral tetracycline at about three months rather than continuing indefinitely
Scarring, nodular disease and significant psychological impact all justify escalation to isotretinoin
Topical antibiotics are always paired with benzoyl peroxide to limit resistance
Isotretinoin in Australia is a dermatologist authority prescription with mandatory pregnancy prevention
Combined oral contraception is an adjunct for hormonal pattern acne, not a rescue for scarring nodules
explanation.pearls: Isotretinoin is teratogenic through its whole course and for one month after the last dose, so pregnancy must be avoided from one month before starting until one month after finishing, with monthly testing in between.

subtopic_detail: Three weeks of blood streaked sputum in a heavy smoker whose chest radiograph is reported as normal
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 58 year old man who has coughed up streaks of blood in his morning phlegm on most days for three weeks. He describes the amount as a teaspoon at most and says the phlegm is otherwise clear.

He has smoked 25 cigarettes a day since he was 18 and has no diagnosis of chronic lung disease. He has had no fever or purulent sputum at any stage, and his weight and exercise tolerance are unchanged. Examination of his chest is normal with equal breath sounds and a normal voice. A chest radiograph performed yesterday was reported as showing clear lung fields with no mass, effusion or collapse. His full blood examination and coagulation profile are normal and he takes no anticoagulant.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78 per minute, blood pressure 138/84 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 96 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Chest clear with equal air entry, no clubbing, no cervical or supraclavicular lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Full blood examination and coagulation profile normal, chest radiograph reported as normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat the chest radiograph in six weeks and investigate further only if a new abnormality appears
options.rationale: A repeat plain film has the same blind spots as the first, particularly the hila and the central airways where an endobronchial tumour causing haemoptysis typically sits. Interval films are used for resolving consolidation, not for excluding malignancy (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer guidelines).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer guidelines

options.text: Prescribe a course of amoxicillin with clavulanate and reassess him once the treatment is finished
options.rationale: There is no fever, purulent sputum or focal sign to suggest infection, so an antibiotic trial only delays diagnosis by a further fortnight. It would be defensible if he had an acute purulent illness with focal crackles (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).

options.text: Send three early morning sputum specimens for cytology and base further imaging on those results
options.rationale: Sputum cytology has poor sensitivity for peripheral lesions and a negative result cannot exclude a tumour, so it does not alter the need for cross sectional imaging. Its residual role is in patients unfit for any invasive procedure (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer guidelines).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer guidelines

options.text: Attribute the blood to airway irritation from smoking and review him after a cessation attempt
options.rationale: Smoking is the reason to investigate rather than a reason to observe, since it raises the pre test probability of malignancy that this presentation is designed to exclude. Cessation support belongs in the same consultation but not instead of imaging (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer guidelines).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer guidelines

options.text: Arrange contrast enhanced computed tomography of the chest and refer him for respiratory assessment
options.rationale: Haemoptysis persisting beyond a week in a smoker over 40 warrants cross sectional imaging because a normal chest radiograph misses a substantial minority of lung cancers, especially central lesions. Parallel specialist referral allows bronchoscopy to be arranged without waiting for a second general practice review (Source: Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer guidelines).
source_refs: Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer guidelines
RACGP: Red Book, preventive activities in general practice

explanation.summary: Haemoptysis in an older smoker is treated as lung cancer until imaging says otherwise, because a normal chest radiograph provides false reassurance in a meaningful proportion of cases. Central endobronchial tumours are the classic cause of blood streaked sputum and are precisely the lesions a plain film is worst at showing. Computed tomography of the chest defines the airway and the mediastinum and directs whether bronchoscopy or a percutaneous biopsy is the appropriate tissue step. Non malignant causes such as bronchiectasis, tuberculosis, pulmonary embolism and anticoagulant effect are also identified on the same study. Where imaging is normal and bleeding continues, bronchoscopy is still commonly performed in the higher risk age and smoking group.
key_points: A normal chest radiograph does not exclude lung cancer in a patient with haemoptysis
Persistent haemoptysis in a smoker over 40 is an indication for computed tomography of the chest
Central endobronchial lesions are the tumours most often missed on a plain film
Sputum cytology lacks the sensitivity to change management in this setting
Smoking cessation support runs alongside the diagnostic pathway rather than replacing it
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about the volume of blood, since more than about 100 to 200 mL in 24 hours defines massive haemoptysis and changes the pathway to urgent admission with the bleeding side placed down.

sources.label: Cancer Council Australia: Lung cancer guidelines
RACGP: Red Book, preventive activities in general practice

subtopic_detail: Thyrotoxicosis emerging after eighteen months of amiodarone with an avascular gland on Doppler
stem:
You are the medical registrar assessing a 68 year old man referred by his cardiologist. He has taken amiodarone for eighteen months to maintain sinus rhythm after two failed ablations, and over the past six weeks he has lost 7 kg, become heat intolerant and had two documented episodes of rapid atrial fibrillation.

He has no eye signs, no neck pain and no tenderness over the thyroid, and the gland is not enlarged or nodular. He has never lived in an iodine deficient region and has no family history of thyroid disease. His thyroid stimulating hormone is less than 0.01 mIU/L with a free thyroxine of 42 pmol/L. Thyroid receptor antibodies are negative, and colour flow Doppler of the thyroid shows markedly reduced vascularity throughout the gland.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 112 per minute and irregular, blood pressure 142/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air, temperature 37.1 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone less than 0.01 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), free thyroxine 42 pmol/L (10-20), free triiodothyronine 9.8 pmol/L (3.5-6.0), thyroid receptor antibodies negative, C reactive protein 6 mg/L (less than 5)
data_table.Imaging: Colour flow Doppler shows markedly reduced thyroidal vascularity with a normal sized gland

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment for his thyroid disorder?

options.text: Commence carbimazole at high dose and continue it until the free thyroxine has normalised
options.rationale: Thionamides block new hormone synthesis and work in the iodine induced type where the gland is overproducing, which typically shows normal or increased vascularity and often underlying nodularity. They have little effect on hormone already released from a destroyed follicular epithelium (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Cease the amiodarone alone and recheck his thyroid function in six to eight weeks time
options.rationale: Amiodarone has a half life of around 50 days so stopping it produces no useful change over weeks, and the cardiologist may need it continued for rhythm control. Withdrawal alone leaves an actively thyrotoxic man with atrial fibrillation untreated (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Arrange radioactive iodine ablation of the thyroid gland once his heart rate is controlled
options.rationale: The iodine load from amiodarone saturates the gland and suppresses radioiodine uptake for many months, so the treatment cannot be delivered effectively. Radioiodine is a definitive option for Graves disease or a toxic nodule in a patient without recent iodine exposure (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

options.text: Start oral prednisolone at an anti inflammatory dose and taper it as thyroid function improves
options.rationale: Absent vascularity on Doppler with no goitre, no nodules and negative receptor antibodies points to the destructive form, in which preformed hormone leaks from damaged follicles and corticosteroids are the effective treatment. Response is often seen within one to two weeks and supports the diagnosis retrospectively (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Amiodarone and thyroid dysfunction

options.text: Refer him for urgent total thyroidectomy as the definitive management of his thyrotoxicosis
options.rationale: Surgery is reserved for thyrotoxicosis refractory to medical therapy or where cardiac decompensation demands immediate control, and it carries substantial risk in an unprepared thyrotoxic patient. Medical therapy has not yet been trialled here (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology).

explanation.summary: Amiodarone contains a large iodine load and is directly toxic to thyroid follicular cells, so it produces two distinct forms of thyrotoxicosis that require opposite drug treatments. The iodine induced form arises in a gland with pre existing autonomy such as a multinodular goitre and responds to thionamides, while the destructive form occurs in a structurally normal gland and responds to corticosteroids. Colour flow Doppler is the most practical discriminator in Australian practice because radioiodine uptake scanning is uninformative after an iodine load. Mixed forms exist and are treated with both agents, and failure to respond within a couple of weeks should prompt that combination. The decision to continue or stop amiodarone is made jointly with cardiology, since its long half life means cessation changes little in the short term.
key_points: Type 1 disease occurs in an abnormal gland with preserved or increased vascularity and responds to carbimazole
Type 2 disease is destructive, shows absent vascularity in a normal gland and responds to prednisolone
Negative thyroid receptor antibodies and no goitre argue against Graves disease as the driver
The iodine load blocks radioiodine uptake for months, removing that treatment option
Amiodarone has a half life of about 50 days so cessation alone gives no rapid benefit
explanation.pearls: A brisk fall in free thyroxine within one to two weeks of starting prednisolone 30 to 40 mg daily effectively confirms the destructive type, and failure to respond in that window is the trigger to add a thionamide for mixed disease.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia: Amiodarone and thyroid dysfunction

subtopic_detail: Screening for primary aldosteronism in a patient whose general practitioner has already started a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist
stem:
You are the registrar in a hypertension clinic seeing a 52 year old woman referred for investigation of blood pressure that has stayed above target on three agents. Her general practitioner added spironolactone 25 mg daily eight weeks ago as a fourth agent and her readings have improved since.

She also takes perindopril, amlodipine and hydrochlorothiazide. Home readings average 148/92 mmHg. She has never been pregnant, has no snoring or witnessed apnoeas, and her body mass index is 27 kg/m2. She takes no liquorice, no non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs and no decongestants. Renal ultrasound performed by her general practitioner showed two normal sized kidneys with no asymmetry. Her potassium today is 4.2 mmol/L and her creatinine is 74 micromol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 74 per minute, blood pressure 152/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 4.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), sodium 139 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 74 micromol/L (45-90), bicarbonate 27 mmol/L (22-32)
data_table.Medication history: Perindopril, amlodipine, hydrochlorothiazide, and spironolactone 25 mg daily started 8 weeks ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her assessment?

options.text: Measure the aldosterone to renin ratio at the next visit while she continues her current medications
options.rationale: A mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist raises renin substantially and is the classic cause of a falsely normal ratio, so a negative result taken now could not be trusted. Testing on other agents is acceptable with cautious interpretation, but not on spironolactone (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary aldosteronism).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary aldosteronism

options.text: Proceed directly to adrenal vein sampling to establish whether her excess is unilateral or bilateral
options.rationale: Adrenal vein sampling is a lateralisation study performed only after biochemical confirmation, and it is technically demanding and invasive. Undertaking it before a screening ratio inverts the diagnostic sequence (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary aldosteronism).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary aldosteronism

options.text: Request computed tomography of the adrenal glands to look for an adenoma before any blood testing
options.rationale: Non functioning adrenal nodules are common with age and a normal appearing gland does not exclude aldosterone excess, so imaging first misleads in both directions. Imaging follows confirmed biochemistry as part of the lateralisation pathway (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary aldosteronism).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary aldosteronism

options.text: Arrange a seated saline suppression test on her current regimen to confirm autonomous secretion
options.rationale: Confirmatory suppression testing is only undertaken after a positive screening ratio and is subject to the same drug interference from a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist. Performing it now risks a false negative and an incorrect exclusion (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary aldosteronism).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary aldosteronism

options.text: Cease the spironolactone for six weeks, control her pressure with verapamil or prazosin, then screen
options.rationale: Spironolactone must be withdrawn for at least six weeks before the aldosterone to renin ratio is measured, and blood pressure in the interim is held with agents that barely disturb the renin angiotensin axis such as a non dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker or an alpha blocker. Potassium is also normalised before sampling because hypokalaemia suppresses aldosterone secretion (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary aldosteronism).
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary aldosteronism

explanation.summary: Primary aldosteronism accounts for a substantial minority of resistant hypertension and matters because unilateral disease is curable by adrenalectomy and because aldosterone excess causes cardiovascular and renal damage beyond that explained by the blood pressure. Screening uses the aldosterone to renin ratio, which is highly sensitive to the drugs a hypertensive patient is usually taking. Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists and high dose diuretics cause false negatives by raising renin and must be stopped for around six weeks, while beta blockers cause false positives by suppressing it. Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers and dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers can usually be continued if the result is interpreted with those effects in mind. Verapamil, prazosin, moxonidine and hydralazine are the agents used to hold pressure during the washout.
key_points: Spironolactone and eplerenone require about six weeks of withdrawal before the ratio is measured
Beta blockers suppress renin and produce false positive ratios
Verapamil, prazosin, moxonidine and hydralazine are the least interfering antihypertensives during washout
Correct hypokalaemia before sampling because low potassium suppresses aldosterone release
Imaging and adrenal vein sampling follow confirmed biochemistry, never precede it
explanation.pearls: A normal potassium does not argue against primary aldosteronism, since fewer than half of confirmed cases are hypokalaemic and normokalaemic disease is now the usual presentation.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary aldosteronism

subtopic_detail: Ophthalmoplegia with ataxia and areflexia after gastroenteritis when the early cerebrospinal fluid protein is normal
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 46 year old man who has had double vision and an unsteady walk for four days. Ten days before that he had five days of watery diarrhoea after a barbecue.

He cannot follow your finger fully in any direction and both eyelids sit slightly low. His gait is wide based and he cannot heel to toe walk, yet limb power is 5 out of 5 throughout and he can lift his head off the pillow strongly. All deep tendon reflexes are absent and both plantar responses are flexor. He is fully orientated with no confusion and drinks no alcohol. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with contrast is normal. Lumbar puncture performed today shows a protein of 0.38 g/L with one white cell per microlitre, and his forced vital capacity is 3.6 L with a single breath count of 32.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 per minute, blood pressure 134/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Bilateral partial ptosis with restricted eye movements in all directions, wide based ataxic gait, generalised areflexia, limb power 5 out of 5, no sensory level
data_table.Investigations: Cerebrospinal fluid protein 0.38 g/L (0.15-0.45), cerebrospinal fluid white cells 1 x10^6/L (less than 5), forced vital capacity 3.6 L, magnetic resonance imaging of brain with contrast normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Commence intravenous immunoglobulin and monitor his vital capacity and swallow regularly
options.rationale: The triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and areflexia after a diarrhoeal illness is a variant of acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy, and immunoglobulin is given without waiting for confirmatory testing when disability is progressing. Serial vital capacity and bulbar assessment are mandatory because the variant can evolve into generalised weakness with respiratory failure (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).
source_refs: Brain: Fisher syndrome and the anti GQ1b antibody spectrum

options.text: Repeat the lumbar puncture in one week and withhold specific treatment until the protein rises
options.rationale: Cerebrospinal fluid protein is normal in a large proportion of patients in the first week and rises later, so a normal early result never excludes the diagnosis or justifies deferring therapy. Waiting a week discards the window in which immunoglobulin alters the disease course (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Give high dose intravenous methylprednisolone for three days and reassess his eye movements
options.rationale: Corticosteroids have been shown not to improve outcome in this group of post infectious neuropathies and may delay recovery, which distinguishes them from chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy where steroids do work. The clinical near pair here is therefore the chronic form, not this acute one (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Administer high dose parenteral thiamine before any glucose containing fluid is commenced
options.rationale: Ophthalmoplegia and ataxia do occur in the thiamine deficient encephalopathy, but that syndrome features confusion and arises with alcohol dependence or prolonged malnutrition, neither of which is present, and it does not abolish reflexes. Areflexia with a preceding diarrhoeal illness points to the immune neuropathy instead (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology).

options.text: Refer him for urgent thrombolysis assessment on the basis of an acute brainstem ischaemic event
options.rationale: A brainstem stroke produces crossed signs, long tract findings and usually a visible lesion on diffusion weighted imaging, and it does not cause global areflexia over four days. His normal magnetic resonance imaging and subacute course place him outside any reperfusion pathway (Source: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management).
source_refs: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management

explanation.summary: Post infectious immune mediated neuropathies span a spectrum from the classic ascending motor form to variants defined by cranial nerve and cerebellar type involvement, and the variant presenting with ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and areflexia is strongly associated with antibodies to the GQ1b ganglioside. Campylobacter jejuni is the commonest identified antecedent infection in Australia and typically precedes onset by one to three weeks. The pivotal clinical trap is that cerebrospinal fluid protein is normal in most patients tested within the first week, so treatment decisions are made clinically. Immunoglobulin and plasma exchange are equally effective and are chosen on availability and comorbidity, and corticosteroids are ineffective. Monitoring is as important as treatment because roughly a fifth of patients across the spectrum need ventilation.
key_points: Ophthalmoplegia with ataxia and areflexia after a diarrhoeal illness defines the anti GQ1b variant
Normal cerebrospinal fluid protein in the first week does not exclude the diagnosis
Immunoglobulin and plasma exchange are equivalent; corticosteroids are ineffective
Serial forced vital capacity and single breath count detect impending respiratory failure
Preserved limb power does not exclude progression to generalised weakness
explanation.pearls: A forced vital capacity below about 20 mL/kg, or a fall of more than 30 per cent from baseline, is the trigger for intensive care review well before oxygen saturation or blood gases become abnormal.

sources.label: Stroke Foundation: Clinical guidelines for stroke management
Brain: Fisher syndrome and the anti GQ1b antibody spectrum
